newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen unlikely to tighten stock trade rule.
newsitem.headline: China seen unlikely to tighten stock trade rule.

text.p: China's stock markets have been swept by rumours of a clampdown on speculation, but analysts said regulators would not use one of their most feared weapons in the near future because it would send tax revenues tumbling.

Plans to force investors to hold on to stock for three days -- instead of one day currently -- would have a big impact on government tax receipts, and were adamantly opposed by the Ministry of Finance, stock analysts said.

"The proposal has been blocked," said an analyst at China Securities Co. "As I understand it, the Ministry of Finance does not agree with the proposal because it would reduce stock turnover and that in turn would reduce tax revenues."
Other securities analysts took a similar view of widespread speculation over what has been dubbed the T+3 system -- requiring investors to hold shares they buy for three days after the transaction.
The longer holding period would tie up funds and make less money available for further stock trades.
"The main reason they (market regulators) won't go ahead with this is it would reduce tax revenues," said an analyst with J & A Securities.
"The tax loss would be almost eight billion yuan ($960 million) this year."
China earned 12.6 billion yuan from securities stamp duty last year, and analysts estimate that without a switch to T+3 the total would top 20 billion yuan this year.
The duty was raised in May this year to 0.5 percent of the value of the stock from 0.3 percent.
Stamp tax receipts in May reached 3.67 billion yuan -- 10 times the total for the same month last year, state media said.

The State Administration of Taxation had no comment on the T+3 system. But tax officials said 80 percent of the stock stamp tax receipts went to the central government and 20 percent to the local governments in Shanghai and Shenzhen -- where the nation's two stock exchanges are located.
Other analysts said the weakness of China's stock markets also weighed against any quick move to extend the stock holding period for investors.

In the week since Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule, China's share markets have stumbled badly. Shanghai's index of A shares for domestic investors had slid more than 14 percent by midday on Tuesday and Shenzhen A shares had fallen more than 18 percent.
"The stock market is weak now and it would not be a good time to implement T+3," said Wang Zheng of Fujian Xingye Securities.
Wang also suggested that the enforcement mechanisms might not be up to the task.
"Shanghai has done a fairly good job of enforcing the T+1 system but Shenzhen has been less effective," he added. "Enforcing T+3 would be even more difficult."
